# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, in full under 10,000 (0 / 1,000 / 2,000) and
  compact on an axis that reaches it (0 / 10K / 20K), one style per axis; along a
  horizontal axis, in full under a million where the labels fit side by side. They
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: white or
  near-black, the same two in both modes, by the fill's luminance. `palette.md` says which its
  categorical and status colors take.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Segmented bar - one whole, split into parts.** A figure, thin or tall, with no baseline, so
  no end is square. Widths proportional to the values; a part at zero draws nothing.
  **Thin:** 8px, or 4px in dense rows; fully rounded ends; no text. **Tall:** 28px and never
  more; each part its own block, 4px corners, its share (46%) or rounded amount (413M)
  printed inside at the leading edge, in white or near-black (*Labels & legend* says which).
  A block too narrow for its label prints none: that value stays in the table view or, in a
  static image (no hover, no table view), goes beside the part's name in the legend.
  Hover, keyboard focus, and the bar's accessible name give every part's name, amount, and
  share. The legend lists the names in block order and repeats no number a block prints. The tall bar is
  exempt from four chart rules: the 24px bar cap, the ban on large saturated blocks, the ban
  on a number on every point, and direct name labels (its legend names the parts). It keeps
  its legend and its table view.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)</result>

  no end is square. Widths proportional to the values; a part at zero draws nothing.

  static image (no hover, no table view), goes beside the part's name in the legend.
  Hover, keyboard focus, and the bar's accessible name give every part's name, amount, and
  share. The legend lists the names in block order and repeats no number a block prints. The tall bar is
  exempt from four chart rules: the 24px bar cap, the ban on large saturated blocks, the ban
  on a number on every point, and direct name labels (its legend names the parts). It keeps
  its legend and its table view.

  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.

  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default

  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve

# Anti-patterns - what goes wrong

Check every chart against this list. If your output matches an entry, it is wrong -
fix it before shipping. These are real failure modes, each caught in shipping
dashboards.

## Color & encoding

**Bad: Dual-axis charts (two y-scales on one plot).**
Why it misleads: the alignment of the two scales is arbitrary, so the chart invents a
correlation that isn't in the data. Real example: an "Adoption" chart plotting Users
(0-30k) against Sessions (0-800k) - a reviewer flagged it as looking "hallucinated."
Good: Do instead: two charts, small multiples, or index both series to a common base
(=100 at t0) on **one** axis.

**Bad: Recolor-on-filter.** Assigning colors by current rank, so filtering out a series
repaints the survivors.
Why: a reader who learned "Acme is blue" is now misled.
Good: Color follows the entity, not its row number. Survivors keep their hue.

**Bad: Cycling / generating hues past 8.** A 9th categorical color, generated or reused.
Why: indistinguishable from an existing slot under CVD; breaks the order check.
Good: Fold the tail into "Other," facet into small multiples, or use composite encoding.

**Bad: Eyeballing colorblind-safety.** "These look different enough."
Good: Run `scripts/validate_palette.js`. Adjacent Delta E >= 8 (OKLab ×100), or 6-8 WITH secondary encoding.

**Bad: A value-ramp on nominal categories.** Coloring each bar darker-where-bigger
when the categories have no natural order (products, teams, endpoints).
Why: it double-encodes bar length as hue, burns the only free channel on
information the chart already shows, and fails the categorical checks by design
(a ramp spans the lightness band and drops below the chroma floor).
Good: One series -> one color (slot 1) for every bar. Ordered categories (funnel,
tiers, age bands) -> the ordinal ramp, validated with `--ordinal`.

**Bad: Rainbow / non-neighbor sequential.** A multi-hue ramp for magnitude.
Good: One hue, light->dark. (Analogous neighbors or semantic heat are the only multi-hue
sequential exceptions, always with a scale legend.)

**Bad: A hue at the diverging midpoint, or two cool hues as the two poles.**
Why: the midpoint must read as "nothing"; poles must read as opposite. blue<->aqua
fails this (both cool); blue<->red or blue<->orange succeed (warm/cool).
Good: Two hues that read as opposite + a neutral gray midpoint.

**Bad: Status color used for a non-status series** (or a series color used for status).
Good: Status tokens only when the color *means* good/bad; categorical when it's identity.

## Form

**Bad: Eight categorical hues when the story is one number.** The most common way a
chart misses its point.
Good: Emphasis (highlight one, gray the rest), or a stat tile / hero number.

**Bad: A one-bar bar chart, or a 2-slice pie.**
Good: A stat tile. The number is the chart.

**Bad: A donut/pie for comparing close values.**
Good: Ranked bars, or the numbers. Part-to-whole at a glance only, <= 6 segments: the tall
segmented bar (`choosing-a-form.md`).

**Bad: More than ~7 color classes carrying meaning.**
Good: A table, or table + chart. Past ~7 bins, adjacent classes blur.

## Marks & chrome

**Bad: Thick saturated blocks, heavy gridlines, no breathing room.** Reads loud, even
childish, at scale.
Good: Thin marks, hairline recessive grid/axes, generous padding. Saturated fills are
for small marks and accents, never large blocks.
**Exception:** the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `marks-and-anatomy.md`).

**Bad: Dashed gridlines or axis rules.** Dashing adds visual noise and reads as
"projection" or "threshold" when it's just a grid.
Good: Gridlines and axes are solid hairlines, one shade off the surface.

**Bad: A number on every data point.** A value beside every dot or segment is chaos and goes unread.
Good: A legend is always present for >= 2 series; direct-label *selectively* (the endpoint, the extreme, the one series that matters) and let the axis + tooltip carry the rest.
**Exception:** the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `marks-and-anatomy.md`).

**Bad: A border drawn around marks to separate them.**</result>
</event>

const analyze = `"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after both benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \\

"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after both benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
        python -I bench/analyze.py

Reads   bench/results/{musicrs,pymusic}.csv  (one row per timed call)
Writes  bench/results/summary.csv            (every statistic, machine-readable)
        bench/results/summary.md             (the tables in the README)
        docs/benchmark{,-dark}.svg           (mean ± stddev bar chart)
        docs/benchmark-distribution{,-dark}.svg  (histograms of t / median)

Scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency changes) only ever adds time, so it shows
up as a right tail: mean > median, positive skew and a few slow outliers. Besides mean,
stddev and median, the summary therefore reports
  * the spread around the median (MAD, p5/p95, min/max),
  * the shape (skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether
    a normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC),
  * outliers: calls slower than median + 3 * 1.4826 * MAD (3 robust sigmas), their share,
    and how much they raise the mean ("tail excess": mean of all calls over the mean of the
    calls that are not outliers).
"""

import math
import os
from collections import defaultdict

DOCS = "docs"
IMPLS = ["pymusic", "musicrs"]
LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "musicrs": "musicrs"}

    ("narrowband", "Narrowband DOA"),
    ("ifb_one_bin", "IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin"),
    ("ifb_all_bins", "IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins"),
]

                  grid="#e1e0d9", axis="#c3c2b7", musicrs="#2a78d6", pymusic="#eb6834"),
    "dark": dict(surface="#1a1a19", ink="#f0efec", ink2="#c3c2b7", muted="#898781",
                 grid="#2c2c2a", axis="#383835", musicrs="#3987e5", pymusic="#d95926"),

    samples = defaultdict(list)
    for impl in IMPLS:

    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in samples.items()}

    med = float(np.median(t))
    mad = float(np.median(np.abs(t - med))) * 1.4826  # scaled to sigma for normal data
    outliers = t > med + 3 * mad if mad > 0 else np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    mean = float(t.mean())
    # Shapiro-Wilk is only defined for 3..5000 samples

        cv=float(t.std(ddof=1)) / mean,

        mad=mad,

await write('bench/README.md', `# Runtime benchmark: musicrs vs pyMUSIC

Times the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC) and musicrs on the
same calls and recordings, keeps every timed call, and summarises the distributions. The
results and charts are in the top-level README, section *Performance vs pyMUSIC*.

## Workloads

All use the 1400 Hz / 40° recordings in \`tests/data/single-source/\` (4 channels, 16 kHz)
and the default estimator (Kinect array, 720 angles over [0, 2π)).

| Workload | pyMUSIC | musicrs | Recordings |
|---|---|---|---|
| \`narrowband\` | \`MUSICEst.getSourceAngles(data, 1, 1400)\` | \`estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)\` | 1 s, 2 s |
| \`ifb_one_bin\` | \`IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=[14])\` | \`ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))\` | 1 s, 2 s |
| \`ifb_all_bins\` | \`IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=range(1, 81))\` | \`ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&(1..=80)))\` | 1 s |

Each call includes everything from the real-valued samples to the result: analytic signal
or STFT, covariance, eigendecomposition and the spectrum. Reading the WAV file is not timed.
\`ifb_all_bins\` lists the 80 non-DC bins explicitly because pyMUSIC's \`bins=None\` would also
include DC and musicrs's would not. It runs on the 1 s recording only: one pyMUSIC call
takes about 11 s, and the cost is the 720-angle spectrum per bin, not the recording length.

+All use the 1400 Hz / 40° recordings in `tests/data/single-source/` (4 channels, 16 kHz)
+and the default estimator (Kinect array, 720 angles over [0, 2π)).
+Each call includes everything from the real-valued samples to the result: analytic signal

+include DC and musicrs's would not. It runs on the 1 s recording only: one pyMUSIC call
+takes about 11 s, and the cost is the 720-angle spectrum per bin, not the recording length.

+shape of the distribution, because scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency
+changes) only ever adds time and so appears as a right tail rather than as symmetric

+  *tail excess*, how much they raise the mean over the mean of the other calls.

"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after both benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
        python -I bench/analyze.py

Reads   bench/results/{musicrs,pymusic}.csv  (one row per timed call)
Writes  bench/results/summary.csv            (every statistic, machine-readable)
        bench/results/summary.md             (the tables in the README)
        docs/benchmark{,-dark}.svg           (mean ± stddev bar chart)
        docs/benchmark-distribution{,-dark}.svg  (histograms of t / median)

Scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency changes) only ever adds time, so it shows
up as a right tail: mean > median, positive skew and a few slow outliers. Besides mean,
stddev and median, the summary therefore reports
  * the spread around the median (MAD, p5/p95, min/max),
  * the shape (skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether
    a normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC),
  * outliers: calls slower than median + 3 * 1.4826 * MAD (3 robust sigmas), their share,
    and how much they raise the mean ("tail excess": mean of all calls over the mean of the
    calls that are not outliers).
"""

import csv
import math
import os
from collections import defaultdict

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("svg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
from scipy import stats  # noqa: E402

RESULTS = "bench/results"
DOCS = "docs"
IMPLS = ["pymusic", "musicrs"]
LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "musicrs": "musicrs"}
WORKLOADS = [
    ("narrowband", "Narrowband DOA"),
    ("ifb_one_bin", "IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin"),
    ("ifb_all_bins", "IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins"),
]

# Reference palette of the dataviz method: categorical slots 1 and 2, chart chrome and ink
THEMES = {
    "light": dict(surface="#fcfcfb", ink="#0b0b0b", ink2="#52514e", muted="#898781",
                  grid="#e1e0d9", axis="#c3c2b7", musicrs="#2a78d6", pymusic="#eb6834"),
    "dark": dict(surface="#1a1a19", ink="#f0efec", ink2="#c3c2b7", muted="#898781",
                 grid="#2c2c2a", axis="#383835", musicrs="#3987e5", pymusic="#d95926"),
}


def load():
    samples = defaultdict(list)
    for impl in IMPLS:
        with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, f"{impl}.csv")) as f:
            for row in csv.DictReader(f):
                samples[(impl, row["workload"], row["recording_s"])].append(float(row["seconds"]))
    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in samples.items()}


def describe(t):
    med = float(np.median(t))
    mad = float(np.median(np.abs(t - med))) * 1.4826  # scaled to sigma for normal data
    outliers = t > med + 3 * mad if mad > 0 else np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    mean = float(t.mean())
    # Shapiro-Wilk is only defined for 3..5000 samples
    sw = t[:5000]
    p_norm = float(stats.shapiro(sw).pvalue)
    p_lognorm = float(stats.shapiro(np.log(sw)).pvalue)
    # AIC of maximum-likelihood fits (2 parameters each; log-normal with loc fixed at 0)
    mu, sd = stats.norm.fit(t)
    aic_norm = 4 - 2 * stats.norm.logpdf(t, mu, sd).sum()
    shape, _, scale = stats.lognorm.fit(t, floc=0)
    aic_lognorm = 4 - 2 * stats.lognorm.logpdf(t, shape, 0, scale).sum()
    return dict(
        n=len(t),
        mean=mean,
        std=float(t.std(ddof=1)),
        cv=float(t.std(ddof=1)) / mean,
        median=med,
        mad=mad,
        min=float(t.min()),
        p5=float(np.percentile(t, 5)),
        p95=float(np.percentile(t, 95)),
        max=float(t.max()),
        skew=float(stats.skew(t)),
        kurtosis=float(stats.kurtosis(t)),
        shapiro_p_normal=p_norm,
        shapiro_p_lognormal=p_lognorm,
        better_fit="log-normal" if aic_lognorm < aic_norm else "normal",
        outlier_share=float(outliers.mean()),
        tail_excess=mean / float(t[~outliers].mean()) - 1,
    )


def shape_verdict(s):
    """One phrase for the README table."""
    if s["shapiro_p_normal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with normal"
    if s["shapiro_p_lognormal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with log-normal"
    tail = "right-skewed" if s["skew"] > 0.5 else "skewed left" if s["skew"] < -0.5 else "near-symmetric"
    heavy = ", heavy tail" if s["kurtosis"] > 3 else ""
    return f"{tail}{heavy}, not normal (closer to {s['better_fit']})"


def fmt_time(x):
    if x >= 1:
        return f"{x:.2f} s"
    if x >= 1e-3:
        return f"{x * 1e3:.3g} ms" if x * 1e3 < 100 else f"{x * 1e3:.0f} ms"
    return f"{x * 1e6:.0f} µs"


def cases(samples):
    """(workload key, label, recording) in display order, for the cases both sides ran."""
    out = []
    for key, label in WORKLOADS:
        for rec in sorted({r for (_, w, r) in samples if w == key}):
            if all((impl, key, rec) in samples for impl in IMPLS):
                out.append((key, f"{label} · {float(rec):g} s recording", rec))
    return out


def style(ax, th):
    ax.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(th["axis"])
    ax.tick_params(colors=th["muted"], length=0, labelsize=9)


def bar_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 0.95 * len(rows) + 1.3), dpi=100)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    style(ax, th)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.grid(axis="x", which="major", color=th["grid"], linewidth=1)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

    bar_h = 0.3  # ~22 px at this size: under the 24 px cap
    lo = 1e-4
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        y0 = len(rows) - 1 - i
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            y = y0 + (0.17 if j == 0 else -0.17)
            ax.barh(y, s["mean"] - lo, left=lo, height=bar_h, color=th[impl], linewidth=0)
            # ±1 stddev whisker; the lower end is clipped to the fastest call
            left = max(s["mean"] - s["std"], s["min"])
            ax.plot([left, s["mean"] + s["std"]], [y, y], color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1.2,
                    solid_capstyle="butt")
            ax.text(s["mean"] + s["std"], y, f"  {fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])}",
                    va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=th["ink2"])
        speedup = summary[("pymusic", key, rec)]["mean"] / summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        ax.text(1.0, y0, f"{speedup:,.0f}× faster", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
                va="center", ha="right", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])

    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([r[1] for r in reversed(rows)], fontsize=9.5, color=th["ink"])
    ax.set_xlim(lo, 3e3)
    ticks = [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks)
    ax.set_xticklabels(["0.1 ms", "1 ms", "10 ms", "100 ms", "1 s", "10 s"])
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(matplotlib.ticker.NullLocator())
    ax.set_xlabel("Time per call, log scale (bar: mean, whisker: ± 1 stddev)",
                  color=th["muted"], fontsize=9)
    handles = [matplotlib.patches.Patch(color=th[impl], label=LABEL[impl]) for impl in IMPLS]
    leg = ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), ncol=2,
                    frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, handlelength=1, handleheight=1)
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color(th["ink"])
    fig.suptitle("Runtime per call: musicrs vs pyMUSIC", x=0.01, ha="left",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="semibold", color=th["ink"])
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), 2, figsize=(8.4, 1.45 * len(rows) + 0.9), dpi=100,
                             sharex=True)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    edges = np.linspace(0.8, 2.0, 61)  # t / median, overflow folded into the last bin
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            style(ax, th)
            ax.set_yticks([])
            t = samples[(impl, key, rec)]
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            rel = np.clip(t / s["median"], edges[0], edges[-1] - 1e-9)
            ax.hist(rel, bins=edges, color=th[impl], linewidth=0, rwidth=0.85)
            ax.axvline(1.0, color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1)
            ax.axvline(s["mean"] / s["median"], color=th["ink"], linewidth=1, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
            ax.text(0.99, 0.92,
                    f"n = {s['n']}  ·  CV {s['cv']:.1%}\nskew {s['skew']:.1f}  ·  outliers {s['outlier_share']:.1%}",
                    transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=7.5, color=th["ink2"])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=9, color=th["ink"], pad=3)
            if i == 0:
                ax.text(0, 1.32, LABEL[impl], transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5,
                        fontweight="semibold", color=th["ink"])
    for ax in axes[-1]:
        ax.set_xticks([0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0])
        ax.set_xticklabels(["0.8", "1 = median", "1.2", "1.4", "1.6", "1.8", "≥ 2"])
        ax.set_xlabel("time / median  (solid line: median, dotted: mean)", color=th["muted"], fontsize=8.5)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def write_tables(samples, summary):
    keys = list(next(iter(summary.values())).keys())
    with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, "summary.csv"), "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["implementation", "workload", "recording_s", *keys])
        for (impl, key, rec), s in sorted(summary.items()):
            w.writerow([impl, key, rec, *[s[k] for k in keys]])

    lines = ["| Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) |",
             "|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for key, label, rec in cases(samples):
        speedup = summary[("pymusic", key, rec)]["mean"] / summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            lines.append(
                f"| {label if impl == IMPLS[0] else ''} | {LABEL[impl]} | {s['n']} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])} | {fmt_time(s['median'])} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['p5'])} – {fmt_time(s['p95'])} | {s['cv']:.1%} | "
                f"{f'{speedup:,.0f}×' if impl == 'musicrs' else ''} |")
    lines += ["", "| Workload | Implementation | Shape | Skew | Excess kurtosis | Shapiro p (t / log t) | (Mean − median) / median | Outliers | Tail excess |",
              "|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]

DOCS = "docs"

LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "musicrs": "musicrs"}

    ax.set_yticklabels([r[1] for r in reversed(rows)], fontsize=9.5, color=th["ink"])

    ticks = [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks)
    ax.set_xticklabels(["0.1 ms", "1 ms", "10 ms", "100 ms", "1 s", "10 s"])
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(matplotlib.ticker.NullLocator())
    ax.set_xlabel("Time per call, log scale (bar: mean, whisker: ± 1 stddev)",

                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])

    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})

def distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), 2, figsize=(8.4, 1.45 * len(rows) + 0.9), dpi=100,
                             sharex=True)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    edges = np.linspace(0.8, 2.0, 61)  # t / median, overflow folded into the last bin
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            style(ax, th)
            ax.set_yticks([])
            t = samples[(impl, key, rec)]
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            rel = np.clip(t / s["median"], edges[0], edges[-1] - 1e-9)
            ax.hist(rel, bins=edges, color=th[impl], linewidth=0, rwidth=0.85)
            ax.axvline(1.0, color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1)
            ax.axvline(s["mean"] / s["median"], color=th["ink"], linewidth=1, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
            ax.text(0.99, 0.92,
                    f"n = {s['n']}  ·  CV {s['cv']:.1%}\nskew {s['skew']:.1f}  ·  outliers {s['outlier_share']:.1%}",
                    transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=7.5, color=th["ink2"])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=9, color=th["ink"], pad=3)
            if i == 0:
                ax.text(0, 1.32, LABEL[impl], transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5,
                        fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    for ax in axes[-1]:
        ax.set_xticks([0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0])
        ax.set_xticklabels(["0.8", "1 = median", "1.2", "1.4", "1.6", "1.8", "≥ 2"])
        ax.set_xlabel("time / median  (solid line: median, dotted: mean)", color=th["muted"], fontsize=8.5)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def write_tables(samples, summary):
    keys = list(next(iter(summary.values())).keys())
    with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, "summary.csv"), "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["implementation", "workload", "recording_s", *keys])
        for (impl, key, rec), s in sorted(summary.items()):
            w.writerow([impl, key, rec, *[s[k] for k in keys]])

    lines = ["| Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) |",
             "|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for key, label, rec in cases(samples):
        speedup = summary[("pymusic", key, rec)]["mean"] / summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            lines.append(
                f"| {label if impl == IMPLS[0] else ''} | {LABEL[impl]} | {s['n']} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])} | {fmt_time(s['median'])} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['p5'])} – {fmt_time(s['p95'])} | {s['cv']:.1%} | "
                f"{f'{speedup:,.0f}×' if impl == 'musicrs' else ''} |")
    lines += ["", "| Workload | Implementation | Shape | Skew | Excess kurtosis | Shapiro p (t / log t) | (Mean − median) / median | Outliers | Tail excess |",
              "|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for key, label, rec in cases(samples):
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            lines.append(
                f"| {label if impl == IMPLS[0] else ''} | {LABEL[impl]} | {shape_verdict(s)} | "
                f"{s['skew']:.2f} | {s['kurtosis']:.1f} | "
                f"{s['shapiro_p_normal']:.2g} / {s['shapiro_p_lognormal']:.2g} | "
                f"{(s['mean'] - s['median']) / s['median']:+.1%} | {s['outlier_share']:.1%} | "
                f"{s['tail_excess']:+.1%} |")
    with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, "summary.md"), "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print("\n".join(lines))


def main():
    plt.rcParams.update({"svg.fonttype": "none", "svg.hashsalt": "musicrs-bench",
                         "font.family": "sans-serif"})
    samples = load()
    summary = {k: describe(v) for k, v in samples.items()}
    write_tables(samples, summary)
    os.makedirs(DOCS, exist_ok=True)
    for theme in THEMES:
        suffix = "" if theme == "light" else "-dark"
        bar_chart(samples, summary, theme, os.path.join(DOCS, f"benchmark{suffix}.svg"))
        distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme,
                           os.path.join(DOCS, f"benchmark-distribution{suffix}.svg"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after both benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
        python -I bench/analyze.py

Reads   bench/results/{musicrs,pymusic}.csv  (one row per timed call)
Writes  bench/results/summary.csv            (every statistic, machine-readable)
        bench/results/summary.md             (the tables in the README)
        docs/benchmark{,-dark}.svg           (mean ± stddev bar chart)
        docs/benchmark-distribution{,-dark}.svg  (histograms of t / median)

Scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency changes) only ever adds time, so it shows
up as a right tail: mean > median, positive skew and a few slow outliers. Besides mean,
stddev and median, the summary therefore reports
  * the spread around the median (MAD, p5/p95, min/max),
  * the shape (skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether
    a normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC),
  * outliers: calls slower than median + 3 * 1.4826 * MAD (3 robust sigmas), their share,
    and how much they raise the mean ("tail excess": mean of all calls over the mean of the
    calls that are not outliers).
"""

import csv
import math
import os
from collections import defaultdict

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("svg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
from scipy import stats  # noqa: E402

RESULTS = "bench/results"
DOCS = "docs"
IMPLS = ["pymusic", "musicrs"]
LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "musicrs": "musicrs"}
WORKLOADS = [
    ("narrowband", "Narrowband DOA"),
    ("ifb_one_bin", "IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin"),
    ("ifb_all_bins", "IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins"),
]

# Reference palette of the dataviz method: categorical slots 1 and 2, chart chrome and ink
THEMES = {
    "light": dict(surface="#fcfcfb", ink="#0b0b0b", ink2="#52514e", muted="#898781",
                  grid="#e1e0d9", axis="#c3c2b7", musicrs="#2a78d6", pymusic="#eb6834"),
    "dark": dict(surface="#1a1a19", ink="#f0efec", ink2="#c3c2b7", muted="#898781",
                 grid="#2c2c2a", axis="#383835", musicrs="#3987e5", pymusic="#d95926"),
}


def load():
    samples = defaultdict(list)
    for impl in IMPLS:
        with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, f"{impl}.csv")) as f:
            for row in csv.DictReader(f):
                samples[(impl, row["workload"], row["recording_s"])].append(float(row["seconds"]))
    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in samples.items()}


def describe(t):
    med = float(np.median(t))
    mad = float(np.median(np.abs(t - med))) * 1.4826  # scaled to sigma for normal data
    outliers = t > med + 3 * mad if mad > 0 else np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    mean = float(t.mean())
    # Shapiro-Wilk is only defined for 3..5000 samples
    sw = t[:5000]
    p_norm = float(stats.shapiro(sw).pvalue)
    p_lognorm = float(stats.shapiro(np.log(sw)).pvalue)
    # AIC of maximum-likelihood fits (2 parameters each; log-normal with loc fixed at 0)
    mu, sd = stats.norm.fit(t)
    aic_norm = 4 - 2 * stats.norm.logpdf(t, mu, sd).sum()
    shape, _, scale = stats.lognorm.fit(t, floc=0)
    aic_lognorm = 4 - 2 * stats.lognorm.logpdf(t, shape, 0, scale).sum()
    return dict(
        n=len(t),
        mean=mean,
        std=float(t.std(ddof=1)),
        cv=float(t.std(ddof=1)) / mean,
        median=med,
        mad=mad,
        min=float(t.min()),
        p5=float(np.percentile(t, 5)),
        p95=float(np.percentile(t, 95)),
        max=float(t.max()),
        skew=float(stats.skew(t)),
        kurtosis=float(stats.kurtosis(t)),
        shapiro_p_normal=p_norm,
        shapiro_p_lognormal=p_lognorm,
        better_fit="log-normal" if aic_lognorm < aic_norm else "normal",
        outlier_share=float(outliers.mean()),
        tail_excess=mean / float(t[~outliers].mean()) - 1,
    )


def shape_verdict(s):
    """One phrase for the README table."""
    if s["shapiro_p_normal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with normal"
    if s["shapiro_p_lognormal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with log-normal"
    tail = "right-skewed" if s["skew"] > 0.5 else "skewed left" if s["skew"] < -0.5 else "near-symmetric"
    heavy = ", heavy tail" if s["kurtosis"] > 3 else ""
    return f"{tail}{heavy}, not normal (closer to {s['better_fit']})"


def fmt_time(x):
    if x >= 1:
        return f"{x:.2f} s"
    if x >= 1e-3:
        return f"{x * 1e3:.3g} ms" if x * 1e3 < 100 else f"{x * 1e3:.0f} ms"
    return f"{x * 1e6:.0f} µs"


def cases(samples):
    """(workload key, label, recording) in display order, for the cases both sides ran."""
    out = []
    for key, label in WORKLOADS:
        for rec in sorted({r for (_, w, r) in samples if w == key}):
            if all((impl, key, rec) in samples for impl in IMPLS):
                out.append((key, f"{label} · {float(rec):g} s recording", rec))
    return out


def style(ax, th):
    ax.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(th["axis"])
    ax.tick_params(colors=th["muted"], length=0, labelsize=9)


def bar_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 0.95 * len(rows) + 1.3), dpi=100)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    style(ax, th)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.grid(axis="x", which="major", color=th["grid"], linewidth=1)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

    bar_h = 0.3  # ~22 px at this size: under the 24 px cap
    lo = 1e-4
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        y0 = len(rows) - 1 - i
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            y = y0 + (0.17 if j == 0 else -0.17)
            ax.barh(y, s["mean"] - lo, left=lo, height=bar_h, color=th[impl], linewidth=0)
            # ±1 stddev whisker; the lower end is clipped to the fastest call
            left = max(s["mean"] - s["std"], s["min"])
            ax.plot([left, s["mean"] + s["std"]], [y, y], color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1.2,
                    solid_capstyle="butt")
            ax.text(s["mean"] + s["std"], y, f"  {fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])}",
                    va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=th["ink2"])
        speedup = summary[("pymusic", key, rec)]["mean"] / summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        ax.text(1.0, y0, f"{speedup:,.0f}× faster", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
                va="center", ha="right", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])

    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([r[1] for r in reversed(rows)], fontsize=9.5, color=th["ink"])
    ax.set_xlim(lo, 3e3)
    ticks = [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks)
    ax.set_xticklabels(["0.1 ms", "1 ms", "10 ms", "100 ms", "1 s", "10 s"])
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(matplotlib.ticker.NullLocator())
    ax.set_xlabel("Time per call, log scale (bar: mean, whisker: ± 1 stddev)",
                  color=th["muted"], fontsize=9)
    handles = [matplotlib.patches.Patch(color=th[impl], label=LABEL[impl]) for impl in IMPLS]
    leg = ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), ncol=2,
                    frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, handlelength=1, handleheight=1)
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color(th["ink"])
    fig.suptitle("Runtime per call: musicrs vs pyMUSIC", x=0.01, ha="left",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), 2, figsize=(8.4, 1.45 * len(rows) + 0.9), dpi=100,
                             sharex=True)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    edges = np.linspace(0.8, 2.0, 61)  # t / median, overflow folded into the last bin
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            style(ax, th)
            ax.set_yticks([])
            t = samples[(impl, key, rec)]
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            rel = np.clip(t / s["median"], edges[0], edges[-1] - 1e-9)
            ax.hist(rel, bins=edges, color=th[impl], linewidth=0, rwidth=0.85)
            ax.axvline(1.0, color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1)

"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after both benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
        python -I bench/analyze.py

Reads   bench/results/{musicrs,pymusic}.csv  (one row per timed call)
Writes  bench/results/summary.csv            (every statistic, machine-readable)
        bench/results/summary.md             (the tables in the README)
        docs/benchmark{,-dark}.svg           (mean ± stddev bar chart)
        docs/benchmark-distribution{,-dark}.svg  (histograms of t / median)

Scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency changes) only ever adds time, so it shows
up as a right tail: mean > median, positive skew and a few slow outliers. Besides mean,
stddev and median, the summary therefore reports
  * the spread around the median (MAD, p5/p95, min/max),
  * the shape (skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether
    a normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC),
  * outliers: calls slower than median + 3 * 1.4826 * MAD (3 robust sigmas), their share,
    and how much they raise the mean ("tail excess": mean of all calls over the mean of the
    calls that are not outliers).
"""

import csv
import math
import os
from collections import defaultdict

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("svg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
from scipy import stats  # noqa: E402

RESULTS = "bench/results"
DOCS = "docs"
IMPLS = ["pymusic", "musicrs"]
LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "musicrs": "musicrs"}
WORKLOADS = [
    ("narrowband", "Narrowband DOA"),
    ("ifb_one_bin", "IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin"),
    ("ifb_all_bins", "IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins"),
]

# Reference palette of the dataviz method: categorical slots 1 and 2, chart chrome and ink
THEMES = {
    "light": dict(surface="#fcfcfb", ink="#0b0b0b", ink2="#52514e", muted="#898781",
                  grid="#e1e0d9", axis="#c3c2b7", musicrs="#2a78d6", pymusic="#eb6834"),
    "dark": dict(surface="#1a1a19", ink="#f0efec", ink2="#c3c2b7", muted="#898781",
                 grid="#2c2c2a", axis="#383835", musicrs="#3987e5", pymusic="#d95926"),
}


def load():
    samples = defaultdict(list)
    for impl in IMPLS:
        with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, f"{impl}.csv")) as f:
            for row in csv.DictReader(f):
                samples[(impl, row["workload"], row["recording_s"])].append(float(row["seconds"]))
    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in samples.items()}


def describe(t):
    med = float(np.median(t))
    mad = float(np.median(np.abs(t - med))) * 1.4826  # scaled to sigma for normal data
    outliers = t > med + 3 * mad if mad > 0 else np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    mean = float(t.mean())
    # Shapiro-Wilk is only defined for 3..5000 samples
    sw = t[:5000]
    p_norm = float(stats.shapiro(sw).pvalue)
    p_lognorm = float(stats.shapiro(np.log(sw)).pvalue)
    # AIC of maximum-likelihood fits (2 parameters each; log-normal with loc fixed at 0)
    mu, sd = stats.norm.fit(t)
    aic_norm = 4 - 2 * stats.norm.logpdf(t, mu, sd).sum()
    shape, _, scale = stats.lognorm.fit(t, floc=0)
    aic_lognorm = 4 - 2 * stats.lognorm.logpdf(t, shape, 0, scale).sum()
    return dict(
        n=len(t),
        mean=mean,
        std=float(t.std(ddof=1)),
        cv=float(t.std(ddof=1)) / mean,
        median=med,
        mad=mad,
        min=float(t.min()),
        p5=float(np.percentile(t, 5)),
        p95=float(np.percentile(t, 95)),
        max=float(t.max()),
        skew=float(stats.skew(t)),
        kurtosis=float(stats.kurtosis(t)),
        shapiro_p_normal=p_norm,
        shapiro_p_lognormal=p_lognorm,
        better_fit="log-normal" if aic_lognorm < aic_norm else "normal",
        outlier_share=float(outliers.mean()),
        tail_excess=mean / float(t[~outliers].mean()) - 1,
    )


def shape_verdict(s):
    """One phrase for the README table."""
    if s["shapiro_p_normal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with normal"
    if s["shapiro_p_lognormal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with log-normal"
    tail = "right-skewed" if s["skew"] > 0.5 else "skewed left" if s["skew"] < -0.5 else "near-symmetric"
    heavy = ", heavy tail" if s["kurtosis"] > 3 else ""
    return f"{tail}{heavy}, not normal (closer to {s['better_fit']})"


def fmt_time(x):
    if x >= 1:
        return f"{x:.2f} s"
    if x >= 1e-3:
        return f"{x * 1e3:.3g} ms" if x * 1e3 < 100 else f"{x * 1e3:.0f} ms"
    return f"{x * 1e6:.0f} µs"


def cases(samples):
    """(workload key, label, recording) in display order, for the cases both sides ran."""
    out = []
    for key, label in WORKLOADS:
        for rec in sorted({r for (_, w, r) in samples if w == key}):
            if all((impl, key, rec) in samples for impl in IMPLS):
                out.append((key, f"{label} · {float(rec):g} s recording", rec))
    return out


def style(ax, th):
    ax.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(th["axis"])
    ax.tick_params(colors=th["muted"], length=0, labelsize=9)


def bar_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 0.95 * len(rows) + 1.3), dpi=100)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    style(ax, th)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.grid(axis="x", which="major", color=th["grid"], linewidth=1)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

    bar_h = 0.3  # ~22 px at this size: under the 24 px cap
    lo = 1e-4
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        y0 = len(rows) - 1 - i
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            y = y0 + (0.17 if j == 0 else -0.17)
            ax.barh(y, s["mean"] - lo, left=lo, height=bar_h, color=th[impl], linewidth=0)
            # ±1 stddev whisker; the lower end is clipped to the fastest call
            left = max(s["mean"] - s["std"], s["min"])
            ax.plot([left, s["mean"] + s["std"]], [y, y], color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1.2,
                    solid_capstyle="butt")
            ax.text(s["mean"] + s["std"], y, f"  {fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])}",
                    va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=th["ink2"])
        speedup = summary[("pymusic", key, rec)]["mean"] / summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        ax.text(1.0, y0, f"{speedup:,.0f}× faster", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
                va="center", ha="right", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])

    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([r[1] for r in reversed(rows)], fontsize=9.5, color=th["ink"])
    ax.set_xlim(lo, 3e3)
    ticks = [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks)
    ax.set_xticklabels(["0.1 ms", "1 ms", "10 ms", "100 ms", "1 s", "10 s"])
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(matplotlib.ticker.NullLocator())
    ax.set_xlabel("Time per call, log scale (bar: mean, whisker: ± 1 stddev)",
                  color=th["muted"], fontsize=9)
    handles = [matplotlib.patches.Patch(color=th[impl], label=LABEL[impl]) for impl in IMPLS]
    leg = ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), ncol=2,
                    frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, handlelength=1, handleheight=1)
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color(th["ink"])
    fig.suptitle("Runtime per call: musicrs vs pyMUSIC", x=0.01, ha="left",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), 2, figsize=(8.4, 1.45 * len(rows) + 0.9), dpi=100,
                             sharex=True)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    edges = np.linspace(0.8, 2.0, 61)  # t / median, overflow folded into the last bin
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            style(ax, th)
            ax.set_yticks([])
            t = samples[(impl, key, rec)]
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            rel = np.clip(t / s["median"], edges[0], edges[-1] - 1e-9)
            ax.hist(rel, bins=edges, color=th[impl], linewidth=0, rwidth=0.85)
            ax.axvline(1.0, color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1)
            ax.axvline(s["mean"] / s["median"], color=th["ink"], linewidth=1, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
            ax.text(0.99, 0.92,
                    f"n = {s['n']}  ·  CV {s['cv']:.1%}\nskew {s['skew']:.1f}  ·  outliers {s['outlier_share']:.1%}",
                    transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=7.5, color=th["ink2"])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=9, color=th["ink"], pad=3)
            if i == 0:
                ax.text(0, 1.32, LABEL[impl], transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5,
                        fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    for ax in axes[-1]:
        ax.set_xticks([0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0])
        ax.set_xticklabels(["0.8", "1 = median", "1.2", "1.4", "1.6", "1.8", "≥ 2"])
        ax.set_xlabel("time / median  (solid line: median, dotted: mean)", color=th["muted"], fontsize=8.5)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)

                f"{fmt_time(s['p5'])} – {fmt_time(s['p95'])} | {s['cv']:.1%} | "

Machine: Intel N150 (3 cores), Linux, \`performance\` governor, rustc 1.88, Python 3.10 / numpy 1.23.5; see [\`bench/\`](bench/README.md) for the harnesses and how to reproduce, and [\`bench/results/\`](bench/results/) for the raw samples. ### Distribution of the timings - **Not normal.** Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality for every case (p < 0.001), on t and on log t. Every distribution is right-skewed (skew 1.1 to 3.2, and 16.6 for one case with a single 5× outlier): a sharp edge near the fastest call and a tail of slower ones, the shape of interference that can only add time. A log-normal fits better than a normal in every case, but none is log-normal either. - **Scheduling moves the mean by a few percent.** The mean is at most 4.2 % above the median, and the outliers (calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas) raise the mean by at most 3.8 % (*tail excess*). Mean and median give the same speedups to within a few percent. Because the distributions are skewed, ± stddev overstates the spread below the mean; the p5 – p95 column shows the real range. - **Slow calls come in runs.** Lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.3 to 0.7, so neighbouring calls are alike. Isolated preemptions would hit calls independently; runs point to slower changes in machine state (CPU frequency, caches, the core the process runs on). It is clearest for musicrs IFB-MUSIC with one bin on the 1 s recording: two clusters, ~650 µs and ~790 µs. A re-run reproduced both clusters, in a different order. - **Run to run**, a second musicrs run gave means 3 to 8 % different. Read the numbers as about ± 10 %; the speedups are far larger than that.
Shape statistics per case ${t2} *Outliers*: calls slower than median + 3 · 1.4826 · MAD. *Tail excess*: mean of all calls over the mean without the outliers. *Drift*: mean of the last 10 % of calls over the first 10 %.
`; let readme = await file('README.md').text(); readme = readme.replace('## Differences from pyMUSIC', section + '## Differences from pyMUSIC'); readme = readme.replace(`regenerate them. ## License`, `regenerate them. \`examples/bench_pymusic.rs\` and \`bench/\` hold the runtime benchmark against pyMUSIC; see [\`bench/README.md\`](bench/README.md). ## License`); await write('README.md', readme); ({t2})

# musicrs

Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt
([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for
Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays.

It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written
for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK.

## Features

- Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) →
  pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking.
- Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's
  `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here.
- IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra
  combined by geometric mean.
- FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers.

## Usage

```rust
use musicrs::MusicEstimator;
use nalgebra::DMatrix;

// Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz
let estimator = MusicEstimator::default();

// 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file
let data: DMatrix<f64> = /* ... */;

// Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians
let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0);

// Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins)
let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]));
```

For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval,
sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data,
call `estimate_doa` directly.

### Things to keep in mind

- A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π]
  if you want a single answer.
- IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above
  Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins.
- Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins;
  select the bins that carry signal energy.

## Differences from pyMUSIC

| | pyMUSIC | musicrs |
|---|---|---|
| Eigendecomposition | `np.linalg.eig` (general) | Hermitian solver (`faer`), orthonormal noise basis |
| Sign convention | conjugated analytic signal, `exp(−j2πfτ)` | non-conjugated analytic signal, `exp(+j2πfτ)` (equivalent) |
| Multi-source peaks | broken (see TODO in `getSourceAngles`) | circular local maxima |
| IFB default bins | all, including DC | all except DC |
| Precision | `float128` steering vectors | `f64` |

On nearly noiseless data the noise eigenvalues are degenerate (~1e-15) and `np.linalg.eig`
returns a non-orthogonal noise basis, so pyMUSIC's spectrum values depend on that arbitrary
basis (≈9 % on the test data); its peak locations are unaffected.

## Development

```sh
cargo test                                  # unit, doc and integration tests
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

Test data in `tests/data/single-source/` are 4-channel, 24-bit, 16 kHz WAV recordings named
`single-source_<freq>Hz_<doa>deg_<duration>s.wav`. `tests/golden_test.rs` checks parity with
spectra produced by the original pyMUSIC code; see `tests/golden/generate_golden.py` to
regenerate them.

a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, with pyMUSIC run unmodified. musicrs is **14× to 784× faster** by mean time per call. pyMUSIC spends ~140 ms per pseudo-spectrum building 720 `float128` steering vectors in a Python loop, whatever the recording length, so the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC (one spectrum per bin) and narrows for longer recordings, where musicrs's own work (Hilbert transform, covariance) grows with the sample count. | Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Narrowband DOA · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 159 ms ± 8.03 ms | 158 ms | 150 ms – 173 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 5.63 ms ± 570 µs | 5.41 ms | 5.1 ms – 6.73 ms | 10.1% | 28× | | Narrowband DOA · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 163 ms ± 18.9 ms | 157 ms | 151 ms – 205 ms | 11.6% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 11.7 ms ± 832 µs | 11.5 ms | 11 ms – 13.7 ms | 7.1% | 14× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 144 ms ± 7.19 ms | 142 ms | 139 ms – 157 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 757 µs ± 121 µs | 770 µs | 633 µs – 845 µs | 16.0% | 191× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 152 ms ± 6.85 ms | 151 ms | 143 ms – 164 ms | 4.5% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 1.24 ms ± 94 µs | 1.22 ms | 1.15 ms – 1.44 ms | 7.5% | 122× | | IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 30 | 11.53 s ± 244 ms | 11.43 s | 11.30 s – 11.83 s | 2.1% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 14.7 ms ± 748 µs | 14.5 ms | 13.9 ms – 16.4 ms | 5.1% | 784× | Every call is timed separately (pyMUSIC: 200 calls per case, 30 for 80 bins; A log-normal fits better than a normal in every case, but none is log-normal either. - **Scheduling moves the mean by a few percent.** The mean is at most 4.2 % above the median, and the outliers (calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas) raise the mean by at most 3.8 % (*tail excess*). Because the distributions are skewed, ± stddev overstates the spread below the mean; the p5 – p95 column shows the real range. - **Slow calls come in runs.** Lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.3 to 0.7, so neighbouring calls are alike. # musicrs Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0); // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14])); ``` For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, with pyMUSIC run unmodified. musicrs is **14× to 784× faster** by mean time per call. pyMUSIC spends ~140 ms per pseudo-spectrum building 720 `float128` steering vectors in a Python loop, whatever the recording length, so the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC (one spectrum per bin) and narrows for longer recordings, where musicrs's own work (Hilbert transform, covariance) grows with the sample count. | Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Narrowband DOA · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 159 ms ± 8.03 ms | 158 ms | 150 ms – 173 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 5.63 ms ± 570 µs | 5.41 ms | 5.1 ms – 6.73 ms | 10.1% | 28× | | Narrowband DOA · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 163 ms ± 18.9 ms | 157 ms | 151 ms – 205 ms | 11.6% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 11.7 ms ± 832 µs | 11.5 ms | 11 ms – 13.7 ms | 7.1% | 14× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 144 ms ± 7.19 ms | 142 ms | 139 ms – 157 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 757 µs ± 121 µs | 770 µs | 633 µs – 845 µs | 16.0% | 191× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 152 ms ± 6.85 ms | 151 ms | 143 ms – 164 ms | 4.5% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 1.24 ms ± 94 µs | 1.22 ms | 1.15 ms – 1.44 ms | 7.5% | 122× | | IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 30 | 11.53 s ± 244 ms | 11.43 s | 11.30 s – 11.83 s | 2.1% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 14.7 ms ± 748 µs | 14.5 ms | 13.9 ms – 16.4 ms | 5.1% | 784× | Every call is timed separately (pyMUSIC: 200 calls per case, 30 for 80 bins; # musicrs

Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt
([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for
Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays.

It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written
for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK.

## Features

- Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) →
  pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking.
- Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's
  `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here.
- IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra
  combined by geometric mean.
- FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers.

## Usage

```rust
use musicrs::MusicEstimator;
use nalgebra::DMatrix;

// Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz
let estimator = MusicEstimator::default();

// 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file
let data: DMatrix<f64> = /* ... */;

// Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians
let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0);

// Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins)
let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]));
```

For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval,
sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data,
call `estimate_doa` directly.

### Things to keep in mind

- A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π]
  if you want a single answer.
- IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above
  Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins.
- Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins;
  select the bins that carry signal energy.

## Differences from pyMUSIC

| | pyMUSIC | musicrs |
|---|---|---|
| Eigendecomposition | `np.linalg.eig` (general) | Hermitian solver (`faer`), orthonormal noise basis |
| Sign convention | conjugated analytic signal, `exp(−j2πfτ)` | non-conjugated analytic signal, `exp(+j2πfτ)` (equivalent) |
| Multi-source peaks | broken (see TODO in `getSourceAngles`) | circular local maxima |
| IFB default bins | all, including DC | all except DC |
| Precision | `float128` steering vectors | `f64` |

On nearly noiseless data the noise eigenvalues are degenerate (~1e-15) and `np.linalg.eig`
returns a non-orthogonal noise basis, so pyMUSIC's spectrum values depend on that arbitrary
basis (≈9 % on the test data); its peak locations are unaffected.

## Development

```sh
cargo test                                  # unit, doc and integration tests
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

Test data in `tests/data/single-source/` are 4-channel, 24-bit, 16 kHz WAV recordings named
`single-source_<freq>Hz_<doa>deg_<duration>s.wav`. `tests/golden_test.rs` checks parity with
spectra produced by the original pyMUSIC code; see `tests/golden/generate_golden.py` to
regenerate them.

## License

MIT

# CLAUDE.md

## Project Overview

**musicrs** is a Rust port of the MUSIC (MUltiple SIgnal Classification) algorithm for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone/antenna arrays. Based on R. O. Schmidt's 1986 algorithm and the Python pyMUSIC implementation.

## Commands

```bash
# Build
cargo build
cargo build --release

# Test
cargo test              # all tests except slow ones (#[ignore = "slow"])
cargo test -- --include-ignored   # full suite, including slow tests (CI runs this)
cargo test --lib        # unit tests only
cargo test --test '*'   # integration tests only
cargo test --test golden_test   # parity with the original pyMUSIC spectra
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings   # CI runs this and `cargo fmt --check`

# Documentation
cargo doc --open
```

## Architecture

```
src/
├── lib.rs      # Public API exports and crate-level docs
├── music.rs    # Core MUSIC algorithm (MusicEstimator, spectrum, DOA estimation)
└── stft.rs     # Signal processing (STFT, analytic signal via Hilbert transform)
tests/
├── common/mod.rs                # Shared WAV/filename/angle helpers, ErrorLog
├── integration_test.rs          # Narrowband DOA on every WAV recording (±0.5°)
├── ifb_test.rs                  # IFB-MUSIC on the tone's bin (nfft 160), below Nyquist (±0.5°)
├── golden_test.rs               # Spectra vs. pyMUSIC output; musicrs snapshots at/above Nyquist
├── broadband_test.rs            # IFB-MUSIC on composite multi-tone signals
├── noisy_data_test.rs           # Narrowband DOA with added white noise
├── synthetic_test.rs            # Synthetic plane waves: 2-D arrays, 2–3 sources, no mirror ambiguity
├── golden/                      # pyMUSIC reference CSVs, *.musicrs.csv snapshots, generate_golden.py
└── data/single-source/*.wav     # 4-channel 24-bit 16kHz test recordings
```

**Key types:**
- `MusicEstimator` — main struct; configure antenna positions, angle search range/step, sample rate, and number of sources
- `MusicEstimator::estimate_doa_from_real()` — real-data entry point (analytic signal per channel, then `estimate_doa`), like pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles`
- `MusicEstimator::ifb_music_spectrum()` — wideband variant; bin frequencies use the estimator's `sample_rate`, so tones above Nyquist cannot be recovered
- `select_bins_by_energy()` — picks the IFB bins within N dB of the strongest; with `bins = None` noise-only bins dominate the geometric mean
- `analytic_signal()` — converts real signal to complex via Hilbert transform (FFT-based)
- `stft()` — Short-Time Fourier Transform with configurable window and overlap

**Core algorithm flow:**
1. Compute covariance matrix of complex multichannel input
2. Hermitian eigendecomposition (`faer`) → signal/noise subspace split
3. Compute MUSIC pseudo-spectrum using steering vectors
4. Peak detection → DOA estimates in radians

## Dependencies

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `nalgebra` | Matrix types and linear algebra |
| `num-complex` | Complex number arithmetic |
| `rustfft` | FFT for STFT and Hilbert transform |
| `faer` | Numerically stable Hermitian eigendecomposition |
| `hound` (dev) | Reading WAV test fixtures |
| `approx` (dev) | Floating-point approximate equality in tests |

## Testing

Integration tests load WAV files from `tests/data/single-source/` and compare DOA estimates with the ground truth in the file name. Clean recordings land exactly on the true angle, so their tolerance is one 0.5° grid step; noisy and broadband-triple tests use tolerances set a little above the measured worst error. `common::ErrorLog` prints the worst error per test (`cargo test -- --nocapture`), which is the number to re-check before changing a tolerance. File naming convention:

```
single-source_<freq>Hz_<doa>deg_<duration>s.wav
```

Test data covers:
- Frequencies: 300 Hz – 9.1 kHz (in ~1.1 kHz steps)
- Angles: 0°, 40°, 80°, 120°, 160°
- Durations: 1 s and 2 s
- Array: Kinect 4-mic geometry

## Workflow

- Before implementing a non-trivial change, propose a plan and get it approved first. While planning, ask clarifying questions about anything ambiguous (scope, API shape, defaults, test data) rather than guessing.

- Make changes on a branch, never directly on `main`:
  - `feat/<feature-name>` for new features
  - `fix/<bugfix-name>` for bug fixes
- Structure work in reasonably sized commits: each commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own.
- A project Stop hook (`.claude/settings.json` → `.claude/hooks/run-tests.sh`) runs `cargo test` when a turn ends with changed code under `src/`, `tests/` or `Cargo.*`, and sends failures back to Claude. Tests that take more than ~10 s are marked `#[ignore = "slow"]`, so the hook skips them; run `cargo test -- --include-ignored` for the full suite. Set `MUSICRS_SKIP_HOOK_TESTS=1` before starting Claude Code to turn the hook off.

## Notes

- Rust edition 2024, MSRV follows current stable toolchain
- No `rustfmt.toml` or `clippy.toml` — use `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` defaults
- Golden files: `*.eigh.csv` (pyMUSIC with `np.linalg.eigh`) must match value-by-value; `*.eig.csv` (pyMUSIC as published) only by peak location, because `np.linalg.eig` returns a non-orthogonal noise basis on this near-noiseless data. Regenerate with the command in `tests/golden/generate_golden.py`.
- Snapshot files: `*.narrowband.musicrs.csv` in `tests/golden/` are musicrs's own narrowband spectra at and above Nyquist (8000 Hz, 9100 Hz), not pyMUSIC references (musicrs deliberately differs from pyMUSIC there). They pin the at/above-Nyquist steering-vector behaviour to a relative tolerance of 1e-9. After an intended change, regenerate with `MUSICRS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo test --test golden_test` and review the diff.
- Sign convention: musicrs uses a non-conjugated analytic signal with an `exp(+j2πfτ)` steering vector; pyMUSIC conjugates the analytic signal and uses `exp(−j2πfτ)`. Equivalent below Nyquist. The above-Nyquist sign flip and the real steering vector at Nyquist are musicrs additions tuned to the test data.

content.text:
The benchmark is done and committed on `feat/pymusic-benchmark`, branched from the fix branch. I haven't pushed it.

**Results** (Intel N150, mean ± stddev per call; pyMUSIC runs unmodified):

| Workload | pyMUSIC | musicrs | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Narrowband DOA, 1 s recording | 159 ms ± 8.0 ms | 5.63 ms ± 0.57 ms | 28× |
| Narrowband DOA, 2 s recording | 163 ms ± 18.9 ms | 11.7 ms ± 0.83 ms | 14× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin, 1 s recording | 144 ms ± 7.2 ms | 757 µs ± 121 µs | 191× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin, 2 s recording | 152 ms ± 6.9 ms | 1.24 ms ± 0.09 ms | 122× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins, 1 s recording | 11.53 s ± 0.24 s | 14.7 ms ± 0.75 ms | 784× |

pyMUSIC spends about 140 ms per spectrum on a Python loop that builds 720 steering vectors, whatever the recording length. That's why the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC and smaller for the longer recording.

**What the distributions show:**
- **Shape:** no case is normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.001 every time), and none is log-normal either, though log-normal fits better. All are right-skewed: a sharp floor near the fastest call and a tail of slower calls.
- **Scheduling influence is small:** the mean is at most 4.2% above the median, and the outliers raise the mean by at most 3.8%. Because the timings are skewed, ± stddev overstates the spread below the mean, so the table in the README also gives p5–p95.
- **Slow calls come in runs:** neighbouring calls are correlated (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.3–0.7). Random preemptions would hit calls independently, so this points to slower changes in machine state such as CPU frequency, caches, or which core the process runs on.
- **One odd case:** musicrs IFB with one bin on the 1 s recording has two clusters, around 650 µs and 790 µs. A re-run reproduced both, in a different order. I haven't found the cause.
- **Run to run:** a second musicrs run gave means 3–8% different, so treat the numbers as about ±10%. That doesn't change the speedups in any meaningful way.

**Added files:**
- **`examples/bench_pymusic.rs`** and **`bench/bench_pymusic.py`:** the two timing scripts. They run the same calls and record every call separately.
- **`bench/analyze.py`:** computes all the statistics and draws the charts.
- **`bench/results/`:** the raw timings, summary tables, and the machine details.
- **`docs/benchmark*.svg`:** the bar chart and the histograms, each in a light and a dark version. The README switches between them to match the viewer's theme.
- **`README.md`:** a new "Performance vs pyMUSIC" section with the charts, the tables and these findings. The shape statistics sit in a collapsible block.
- **`bench/README.md`:** how to reproduce, plus an update to the file layout in `CLAUDE.md`.

Should I push it and open a PR? I'd point it at `fix/doc-and-input-checks` so the diff shows only the benchmark, then retarget it to `main` once #13 is merged.

| IFB-MUSIC 1 bin, 2 s | 152 ms | 1.24 ms | 122× |

- **Stack section:** both descriptions now open with a list of the two PRs and each one's base, with a 👉 marking the PR you're reading.
- **Merge order:** stated in both PRs. Merge #13 into `main` first, then switch #14's base to `main`.
